{{Short description|Space in mathematics and theoretical physics}}
In [[mathematics]] and [[theoretical physics]] (especially [[twistor theory]]), '''twistor space''' is the [[complex vector space]] of solutions of the [[Twistor theory|twistor]] equation <math>\nabla_{A'}^{(A}\Omega_{^{}}^{B)}=0 </math>. It was described in the 1960s by [[Roger Penrose]] and Malcolm MacCallum.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=R. |last1=Penrose |first2=M.A.H. |last2=MacCallum |title=Twistor theory: An approach to the quantisation of fields and space-time |journal=Physics Reports |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=241–315 |date=February 1973 |doi=10.1016/0370-1573(73)90008-2 |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0370-1573%2873%2990008-2|url-access=subscription }}</ref> According to [[Andrew Hodges]], twistor space is useful for conceptualizing the way photons travel through space, using four [[complex number]]s. He also posits that twistor space may aid in understanding the [[asymmetry]] of the [[weak nuclear force]].<ref name="Hodges2010">{{cite book|first=Andrew |last=Hodges|title=One to Nine: The Inner Life of Numbers|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UCuwrtBax7AC&q=weak+force+twistor&pg=PA142|date=2010|publisher=Doubleday Canada|isbn=978-0-385-67266-5|page=142}}</ref>

== Informal motivation ==
In the (translated) words of [[Jacques Hadamard]]: "the shortest path between two truths in the real domain passes through the complex domain."  Therefore when studying four-dimensional space <math>\mathbb{R}^4</math> it might be valuable to identify it with <math>\mathbb{C}^2.</math> However, since there is no canonical way of doing so, instead all [[isomorphism]]s respecting orientation and metric between the two are considered. It turns out that [[complex projective space|complex projective 3-space]] <math>\mathbb{CP}^3</math> parametrizes such isomorphisms together with complex coordinates. Thus one complex coordinate describes the identification and the other two describe a point in <math>\mathbb{R}^4</math>. It turns out that [[vector bundle]]s with [[self-dual connection]]s on <math>\mathbb{R}^4</math>([[instanton]]s) [[bijection|correspond bijectively]] to [[holomorphic vector bundle]]s on complex projective 3-space <math>\mathbb{CP}^3</math>.

==Formal definition==
For [[Minkowski space]], denoted <math>\mathbb{M}</math>, the solutions to the twistor equation are of the form

:<math>
\Omega^A(x)=\omega^A-ix^{AA'}\pi_{A'}
</math>

where <math>\omega^A</math> and <math>\pi_{A'}</math> are two constant [[Weyl spinor]]s and <math>x^{AA'}=\sigma^{AA'}_\mu x^{\mu}</math> is a point in Minkowski space. The <math>\sigma_\mu=(I,\vec\sigma)</math> are the [[Pauli matrices]], with <math>A,A^\prime=1,2</math> the indexes on the matrices.   This twistor space is a four-dimensional complex vector space, whose points are denoted by <math>Z^{\alpha}=(\omega^{A},\pi_{A'})</math>, and with a [[hermitian form]]

:<math>
\Sigma(Z)=\omega^{A}\bar\pi_{A}+\bar\omega^{A'}\pi_{A'}
</math>

which is invariant under the [[special unitary group|group SU(2,2)]] which is a quadruple cover of the [[conformal group]] C(1,3) of compactified Minkowski spacetime.

Points in Minkowski space are related to subspaces of twistor space through the [[incidence relation]]

:<math>
\omega^{A}=ix^{AA'}\pi_{A'}.
</math>

This incidence relation is preserved under an overall re-scaling of the twistor, so usually one works in projective twistor space, denoted <math>\mathbb{PT}</math>, which is isomorphic as a complex manifold to <math>\mathbb{CP}^3</math>.

Given a point <math>x\in M</math> it is related to a line in  projective twistor space where we can see the incidence relation as giving the linear embedding of a <math>\mathbb{CP}^1</math> parametrized by <math>\pi_{A'}</math>.

The geometric relation between projective twistor space and complexified compactified Minkowski space is the same as the relation between lines and two-planes in twistor space; more precisely, twistor space is 

:<math>\mathbb{T} := \mathbb{C}^4.</math> 

It has associated to it the double [[fibration]] of [[flag manifold]]s <math>\mathbb{P}\xleftarrow{\mu} \mathbb{F} \xrightarrow{\nu} \mathbb{M}</math> where <math>\mathbb{P}</math> is the projective twistor space

:<math>\mathbb{P}=F_1(\mathbb{T})=\mathbb{CP}^3=\mathbf{P}(\mathbb{C}^4)</math>

and <math>\mathbb{M}</math> is the compactified complexified Minkowski space
:<math>\mathbb{M}=F_2(\mathbb{T})=\operatorname{Gr}_2(\mathbb{C}^4)= \operatorname{Gr}_{2,4}(\mathbb{C})</math>

and the correspondence space between <math>\mathbb{P}</math> and <math>\mathbb{M}</math> is

:<math>\mathbb{F}=F_{1,2}(\mathbb{T})</math>

In the above, <math>\mathbf{P}</math> stands for [[projective space]], <math>\operatorname{Gr}</math> a [[Grassmannian]], and <math>F</math> a [[flag manifold]]. The [[double fibration]] gives rise to two [[1:1 correspondence|correspondences]] (see also [[Penrose transform]]), <math>c=\nu\circ\mu^{-1}</math> and <math>c^{-1}=\mu\circ\nu^{-1}.</math> 

The compactified complexified Minkowski space <math>\mathbb{M}</math> is embedded in <math>\mathbf{P}_5 \cong\mathbf{P}(\wedge^2\mathbb{T})</math> by the [[Plücker embedding]]; the image is the [[Klein quadric]].
